texts.period: Isin-Larsa period composition, c. 2000 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)
texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: When the storm god's wind is unleashed against Ur, the moon god's city falls: the temple desecrated, the people scattered as slaves, mothers and children dying of hunger — and at last Nanna mourns to Enlil and the city is promised restoration.
summary.zh: 暴風之神之風襲向烏爾，月神之城傾覆：神殿被瀆，民眾被虜為奴，母與子飢餓而死——南納終向恩利爾哀告，城池蒙許復興。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: On the day the storm's order was given, Ur was smitten: its temple looted, its people herded away as captives, its cattle and grain carried off — the city that knew no enemy is stripped bare. The lament's heart is hunger: mothers shut their doors against their children, the river runs with bodies, and Nanna, the moon god, has wrapped his city in silence and gone by boat to another place. Nanna mourns before Enlil; the god of the storm answers that the decree was his, and Ur shall be restored: kingship returns to the city, the temple rebuilt, the people regathered — mourning becomes prophecy of return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.2, the destruction; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.2, the hunger; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.2, the restoration promise; not verbatim.

functions: Memorial liturgy for the fall of Ur III
Prototype of the city-lament genre
Prophecy text of restoration tied to royal ideology

variants.summary: The wider lament over the whole land's fall.

variants.summary: The same genre for Enlil's city.

title.en: The Lament for Sumer and Ur

texts.period: Isin-Larsa period composition, c. 2000 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The lament for Sumer and Urim (ETCSL c.2.2.3)

texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The whole land is visited by the flood-storm: city after city falls — Uruk, Lagash, Umma, Shuruppak — the temples emptied, the land made a wilderness, until the gods restore Sumer and the cities sing again.
summary.zh: 洪水暴風席捲全境：烏魯克、拉加什、烏瑪、舒魯帕克相繼陷落，神殿空虛，大地化為荒野——直至眾神復興蘇美，諸城再啟歡歌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The flood-storm comes on the land by the gods' decree: city after city is named and smitten — Uruk, Lagash, Umma, Shuruppak — temples emptied, houses burned, the black-headed people scattered like sheep. The lament catalogs each city's ruin, then turns: the gods restore Sumer, kingship returns to Ur, and the land is promised the days of abundance again — the lament closes in blessing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.3, the storm over the land; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.3, restoration; not verbatim.

functions: Widest city lament: memorial of the land's fall
Restoration prophecy embedded in liturgy
Performed in the lament festivals of the Isin restoration

variants.name: The lament for Urim
variants.summary: The single-city lament of the same fall.

summary.en: The storm reaches even Enlil's own city: the Ekur defiled, its rites silenced, the shepherd's flock scattered — and Enlil, whom no city may accuse, must be petitioned to restore his own house.
summary.zh: 暴風竟及恩利爾之城：埃庫爾被瀆、祭儀止息、牧群四散——無人可責之神，須被懇求復興其殿。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The storm visits even Nippur: the Ekur defiled, its hymns silenced, its priests scattered; Enlil's own city learns what ruin is. The petition to Enlil is unique in the genre: no god may be accused, so the lament asks the offended lord himself to remember his house — and the restoration of the Ekur restores the world's axis.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.4, the ruin; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.4, the petition; not verbatim.

functions: Lament for the sanctuary of sanctuaries
Theology of petition without accusation

variants.name: The lament for Eridu
variants.summary: The lament of the oldest city.

texts.period: Old Babylonian composition, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)
texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The oldest city, Enki's own, is smitten: the Abzu defiled, wisdom's house emptied — and the lament mourns the first city as mourning one's own mother.
summary.zh: 最古老的城、恩基之城遭劫：阿卜祖被瀆，智慧之殿空虛——哀歌以悼母之情悼第一城。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Eridu, the first of cities, Enki's own seat, is smitten by the storm: the Abzu defiled, wisdom's house emptied, the rites of the oldest temple silenced. The lament mourns the first city as a mother; its restoration is the renewal of the world's beginning — when Eridu lives again, the order of things is re-founded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.6, the ruin; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.6, the restoration; not verbatim.

functions: Lament for the first city and its sanctuary
Restoration theology anchored in origins

variants.name: The lament for Unug
variants.summary: The lament of Uruk in the same series.

texts.period: Old Babylonian composition, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)
texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The city of Inanna and Gilgamesh falls to the storm; the Eanna is defiled and its people scattered — the lament petitions the goddess herself to restore her own city, and Uruk's renewal is promised.
summary.zh: 伊南娜與吉爾伽美什之城遭暴風之劫：埃安那被瀆，民眾四散——哀歌向女神本身祈求復興其城，烏魯克之新生蒙許。

sensitivity.note: Ancient city lament; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The storm falls on Unug, city of Inanna and Gilgamesh: the Eanna defiled, its people scattered, the city of the great wall emptied by decree. The lament petitions the lady of the city herself — she who was smitten must smite back the ruin — and Unug's renewal is promised with her restoration of the Eanna.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.5, the ruin; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.2.5, the petition; not verbatim.

functions: Lament of the Inanna city
Liturgical petition to the city goddess

title.en: The Sumerian King List: Kingship from Heaven
title.zh: 蘇美王表：王權自天而降

texts.period: Compiled OB, based on older lists, c. 1800 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)
texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Kingship was lowered from heaven: in the five cities before the flood, eight kings reigned fantastic reigns of tens of thousands of years until the flood swept them; afterwards kingship came again to Kish and passed through the dynasties down to Isin.
summary.zh: 王權自天而降：洪水之前五城八王，在位動輒數萬年；洪水掃盡其後，王權復臨基什，歷經諸朝，傳至伊辛。

sensitivity.note: Ancient historiographical myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When kingship was lowered from heaven, it was in Eridug: Alulim reigned 28,800 years, Alalgar 36,000 — five cities, eight kings, five sars and more, until the flood swept over the land and kingship was taken to heaven. After the flood kingship came again from on high, to Kish first: long reigns shorten through the dynasties — Kish, Uruk, Ur, Akkad, and again Uruk and Ur — each dynasty named, each king given his years, until the list closes with the kings of Isin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.1, antediluvian section; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.1, postdiluvian dynasties; not verbatim.

functions: Political charter: kingship as heaven-given office
Historiographical frame linking flood, dynasties and legitimacy
Reference text for scribal schools and chronicles

summary.en: A dynastic list in which Lagash's rulers — Ur-Nanshe's line, Gudea's house, the soldier kings of the Gutian interlude — are remembered with their deeds, buildings and wars: city history as sacred memory.
summary.zh: 拉加什王朝記：烏爾南什之系、古蒂亞之家、庫提人插曲中的戰士王——以功業、建築與戰事載入記憶：城邦史即神聖記憶。

sensitivity.note: Ancient chronicle; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The rulers of Lagash are remembered dynasty by dynasty: Ur-Nanshe who built the temples, Gudea who saw his god in a dream, the kings who warred with Umma over the boundary — each reign measured by deeds and buildings. The list closes with the restoration kings, whose piety returned Lagash's worship to its gods — city history told as a sacred ledger of justice and building.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.2, the dynasties; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.1.2, the close; not verbatim.

functions: City dynastic chronicle
Charter of Lagash's temple-building legitimacy

texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Ur-Namma, the king who built the ziggurat and gave the land its laws, dies in battle; his son mourns him, and the king descends to the netherworld where the dead come out to greet him as their lord — a royal descent poem of consolation.
summary.zh: 建神塔、定律法之王烏爾納瑪戰場殞身；其子哀悼，國王下冥，亡者出迎其主——一首慰藉性的王室冥界詩。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ur-Namma, who built the temple and gave the land its measures and laws, falls in battle; his son Shulgi mourns: the shepherd is taken, the city's father is gone. The king descends to the netherworld, and the dead come out to greet him as their lord: he is given his seat among the shades, and his offerings are appointed — the king in the land of the dead keeps his kingdom's order.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.1.2, the death; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.1.2, the descent; not verbatim.

functions: Royal funerary liturgy of the Ur III founder
Theology of the dead king's netherworld reign
Charter of continuing royal offerings

variants.name: The death of Gilgamesh
variants.summary: The heroic prototype of the dead king's enthronement.

title.en: Shulgi's Run from Nippur to Ur
title.zh: 舒爾吉尼普魯烏爾長跑

texts.period: Ur III composition, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Inana (Shulgi cycle, ETCSL c.2.4.2.x)

texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Shulgi boasts that in one day he ran from Nippur to Ur — a hundred miles through the storm — to bring offerings on the New Year; the self-deified king measures his kingship in feats: the run, the writing, the justice.
summary.zh: 舒爾吉自誇一日之間自尼普魯奔至烏爾——穿越風暴的百里之程——為新年奉上祭品；自神化的國王以功業丈量王權：長跑、書寫、正義。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Shulgi, king of Ur, boasts: I ran in the storm from Nippur to Ur in a single day, through the teeming rain, and brought the offerings of the New Year with my own hands. The king's litany of feats continues: I learned the scribal art from the tablet-house, I know the songs and the games, I judge the land's cases with justice — the deified king as the complete man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.2, the run; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.2, the litany; not verbatim.

functions: Manifesto of royal deification in the Ur III state
Charter of the New Year offering journey
School text of the royal-hymn genre

variants.name: Shulgi A (the self-praise)
variants.summary: The companion hymn of the king's praise.

texts.period: Ur III composition, c. 2100 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A praise poem of Shulgi (Shulgi cycle, ETCSL c.2.4.2.x)

texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Shulgi praises himself as the son of Ninsun's line: learned in every scribal art, master of music and games, judge of the land — the king as literate demi-god whose praise was copied in schools for centuries.
summary.zh: 舒爾吉自頌為寧蓀後裔：通曉書吏百藝、精於樂藝棋戲、審判全土——身為有學半神之王的讚歌，為校中傳抄數百年。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Shulgi, king of Ur, claims the pedigree of heroes: born of the line of Ninsun, nourished by Ninlil, he is the lord whom the great gods raised to shepherding the land. His learning is the boast of a new age: from the tablet-house he learned the scribal art entire — Sumerian and the foreign tongue, the songs and the calculations — and the schools copied his praise for centuries after his death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.1, pedigree; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.4.2.1, the learning; not verbatim.

functions: Canonization of the deified king in school curricula
Ideology of the literate king

title.en: Iddin-Dagan's Bride of the New Year

texts.period: Isin dynasty composition, c. 1900 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Inana for Iddin-Dagan (Iddin-Dagan A, ETCSL c.2.5.3.1)

texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The morning of Inanna's festival: the goddess bathed and perfumed takes the hymn's stage — her assembling of the land, the sacred marriage bed prepared, the king blessed — the great liturgy of the goddess as bride of the city.
summary.zh: 伊南娜慶典之晨：沐浴敷香的女神登台——她召集全境、備妥聖婚之床、祝福國王——女神身為城邦新娘的偉大祭儀。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult hymn with sexual imagery in ritual register; presented as literature.

passages.text: On the morning of the festival, Inanna bathes and perfumes herself and takes her seat; the land assembles to her, the stars bow to the morning star, and the city is dressed for her advent. The bed is prepared with the king: the goddess claims her lord for the night of the sacred marriage, and through the union the year's abundance is secured for Isin — the rite sung as the goddess's bride-gift to the land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.5.3.1, the advent; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.5.3.1, the marriage; not verbatim.

functions: Liturgy of the sacred marriage at Isin
Charter of the year's abundance through the royal union
Masterpiece of cult love-lyric

summary.en: In a dream a giant stands by Gudea's bed — a winged storm bird at his feet, a woman with a stylus, a youth with a cornerstone — and the dream is read: Ningirsu orders his temple built, and the ruler obeys to the letter.
summary.zh: 夢中巨神立於古蒂亞榻旁——足下振翅的暴風鳥、執書板的女子、持奠基石的少年——夢解為命：寧吉爾蘇命其建殿，統治者依夢而行。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal inscription narrative; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In his dream a giant stands by Gudea's bed, head to heaven; at his feet a winged storm bird, beside him a woman holding a lapis stylus and tablet, and a youth holding a cornerstone slab — the ruler wakes troubled and seeks the dream's meaning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.1, the dream; not verbatim.

passages.text: Nanshe, lady of divination, reads it: the giant is Ningirsu, who orders his temple built; the storm bird is his weapon; the woman is Nisaba who will draw the plan. Gudea obeys: the temple Eninnu is begun exactly as the dream showed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.1, the interpretation; not verbatim.

functions: Charter of royal building as obedience to dream revelation
Detailed liturgy of temple construction
Cult myth of Ningirsu's Eninnu at Girsu

texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The temple Eninnu rises: materials gathered from every land, the foundations laid on the morning of propitious days, the god installed with a seven-day festival — and the land rests in abundance, the year of the temple's dedication blessed.
summary.zh: 埃寧努神殿落成：建材自萬邦匯聚，擇吉晨奠基，七日慶典迎神入殿——國土休養生息，獻殿之年受福。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal inscription narrative; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Materials come from every land for the Eninnu: cedar from the mountains, gold and lapis from far countries, and the foundations are laid on the propitious morning the omens chose. Ningirsu is installed with a seven-day festival; the land rests, taxes are remitted, and the temple's year is blessed — Gudea's piety rewarded with abundance for Lagash.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.2, the building; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.3.2.2, the consecration; not verbatim.

functions: Consecration liturgy of the Eninnu temple
World-renewal theology of temple dedication
Charter of the pious builder king

title.en: A Hymn to Inana for Hammurabi

texts.period: Old Babylonian composition, c. 1750 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to Inana for Hammu-rabi (ETCSL c.2.8.2.1)

texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The Babylonian dynasty's king is praised in Sumerian: Inana, lady of battle, is hymned in her thunder and beauty, and Hammurabi named her favorite — the old south's language put to work for a new empire's king.
summary.zh: 巴比倫王朝之王以蘇美語受頌：戰爭女神伊南娜之雷霆與美麗入詩，漢謨拉比列名其寵——舊邦之語，為新帝之王所用。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Inana is hymned in her double nature: the terror of battle whose heart is storm, and the beauty whose grace fills the temples — the goddess of both war and desire. The hymn names Hammurabi her chosen: the king of Babylon, beloved of the lady, under whose justice the land finds order — Sumerian sung for a new empire's ruler.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.8.2.1, the goddess; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of ETCSL c.2.8.2.1, the king; not verbatim.

functions: Royal legitimacy hymn in the old language
Continuity of the Inanna hymn genre under Babylon
